title: Linked List
summary: Nodes scattered in memory, each holding a value and the address of the next — O(1) insertion anywhere you already stand, O(n) to get anywhere at all.

analogy.beginner: A treasure hunt. Each clue tells you the value at this spot and where the next clue is hidden. To reach clue 7 you must follow clues 1 to 6 — there is no shortcut. But inserting a new clue between 3 and 4 is trivial: rewrite two notes, and nothing else in the hunt has to move.
analogy.interview: A chain of heap-allocated nodes, each holding a payload and a reference to its successor. Sequential access only: O(n) to reach index i, O(1) to insert or delete given a reference to the predecessor. No contiguity, so no cache locality and per-node object overhead.

intuition:
An array buys O(1) access with contiguity, and contiguity is what makes insertion expensive. A linked list makes the opposite trade: give up contiguity, and inserting becomes rewiring two references instead of shifting a million elements — but finding anything now means walking.

That is the entire comparison, and it is the reason interviewers love linked lists: there is nowhere to hide. Every operation is explicit pointer manipulation, so a linked-list question tests whether you can hold a precise mental model of state changing step by step.

One practical caveat worth knowing: in real systems `ArrayList` beats `LinkedList` far more often than Big-O suggests, because chasing pointers to scattered addresses misses cache on nearly every hop. Java's own `LinkedList` is rarely the right production choice. Its value here is as a *teaching* structure and as the backbone of trees, graphs, LRU caches and adjacency lists.

problemFirst.motivatingProblem: Maintain a playlist where users constantly insert songs in the middle and remove songs, thousands of times a second.

bruteForce.idea: Use an array. Inserting at position 3 of a 10,000-song playlist means shifting 9,997 entries one slot right.
code: // insert 'song' at index 3 in an array-backed playlist
songs[i] = songs[i - 1];   // 9,997 moves for one insertion
bruteForce.whySlow: The array's promise — element i is at base + i × size — is exactly what forces the shift. Keeping that promise is the cost.

problemFirst.observation: The shifting exists only to keep elements adjacent. But nothing about a playlist requires the songs to be adjacent in memory; it only requires knowing what comes next.
problemFirst.leap: Store 'what comes next' explicitly in each node. Insertion becomes two reference assignments — O(1) — at the price of losing O(1) access by position.

howItWorks: **Node** = `{ value, next }`. The list is a reference to the first node (`head`); the last node's `next` is `null`.
**Traverse**: `for (Node cur = head; cur != null; cur = cur.next)`. O(n), and the only way to reach index i.
**Insert after a known node**: `newNode.next = cur.next; cur.next = newNode;` — O(1). Order matters; swap those two lines and you lose the rest of the list.
**Delete after a known node**: `cur.next = cur.next.next;` — O(1).
**Insert/delete at the head**: O(1), which is why a stack is trivially a linked list.
**Dummy head node** — a fake node before the real first one. It removes the 'what if we delete the head?' special case from nearly every problem. Use it by default.
**Doubly linked list** adds a `prev` reference: O(1) deletion given only the node itself, and backwards traversal, for one extra reference per node. This is what makes an LRU cache work.

signals: Frequent insertion/removal at positions you already hold a reference to
No need for random access by index
The problem explicitly says 'linked list' (reverse it, detect a cycle, merge two)
Implementing an LRU cache, adjacency list, or a queue
antiSignals: You need to sort or binary search (needs random access)

complexity.time: Access by index O(n) · Search O(n) · Insert/delete at head O(1) · Insert/delete given the predecessor O(1) · Insert/delete at index i O(n) because you must walk there first
complexity.space: O(n) values plus O(n) references — roughly 2–3× an array's memory for the same ints, once object headers are counted
complexity.why: Everything follows from having no address arithmetic: the only way to reach position i is to follow i links. Conversely, once you are standing at a node, rewiring costs a constant number of assignments no matter how long the list is. Note the asymmetry interviewers probe: 'insert is O(1)' is only true if you already hold the predecessor.

commonMistakes.fix: The rest of the list is lost. Always link the new node forward first. Draw the arrows before typing.

commonMistakes.mistake: Losing the head reference while traversing
commonMistakes.fix: Traverse with a separate cursor variable; never advance `head` itself unless you mean to.
Guard with `cur != null && cur.next != null` — and note that Java's `&&` short-circuits, so order matters.
Use a dummy head node. It removes the special case entirely.

commonMistakes.mistake: Reaching for LinkedList in production code
commonMistakes.fix: `ArrayList` is usually faster even for middle insertion at realistic sizes, because of cache locality. Measure before choosing.

realWorldUses: LRU caches: a doubly linked list gives O(1) move-to-front, paired with a HashMap for O(1) lookup.
Java's `HashMap` uses linked nodes for collision chains.
Undo histories, music playlists, and the free-block lists inside memory allocators and filesystems.
interviewNotes: Draw the pointers on paper before writing code. Nearly every linked-list bug is an assignment done in the wrong order.
Standard toolkit: dummy head, two pointers (fast/slow), and reversal. Most questions are a combination of those three.
Always state whether your solution mutates the input list — interviewers care.

quiz.question: What is the time complexity of accessing the 500th element of a singly linked list?
quiz.explanation: There is no address arithmetic — you must follow 500 `next` references. This is the price paid for O(1) insertion.

options: newNode.next points at newNode itself, and the rest of the list is lost
quiz.explanation: After line 1, `cur.next` IS newNode, so line 2 assigns newNode to its own next — a self-loop, and everything after `cur` is unreachable. Link forward first.

quiz.question: Why does a dummy head node simplify deletion?
options: Every real node then has a predecessor, so deleting the first node needs no special case
quiz.explanation: Deletion needs the predecessor's `next` to rewrite. Without a dummy, the first node has no predecessor and needs separate code — a classic source of bugs.

quiz.question: Both ArrayList and LinkedList insert at the head. Which is faster in practice for 10,000 ints, and why?
options: LinkedList always — it is O(1) vs O(n)
LinkedList is asymptotically better, but ArrayList often wins in practice at small-to-moderate sizes due to cache locality and no per-node allocation
quiz.explanation: O(1) vs O(n) eventually wins, but `System.arraycopy` moves contiguous memory extremely fast while pointer-chasing misses cache on nearly every hop. The honest answer names both effects and says: measure.
